citation.title: Topology Optimization via Frequency Tuning of Neural Design Representations
citation.authors: Nikan Doosti, Julian Panetta, Vahid Babaei
citation.venue: Symposium on Computational Fabrication (SCF '21), October 28-29, 2021, Virtual Event, USA (ACM)
citation.version_coded: Author's version (as posted by the author; ACM Digital Library page returned HTTP 403 to automated access); full text (9 pages, including references) read from a PDF hosted on co-author Vahid Babaei's institutional group page (aidam.mpi-inf.mpg.de/data/pdfs/toftndr.pdf, Max Planck Institute for Informatics). The adjudicator re-read the same PDF in full on 2026-09-24 (HTTP 200, no challenge) and read the compliance values printed in Fig. 6 (p. 7) and Figs. 2-5 (pp. 5-6) on the rendered pages

included.reason: I-QUALITY (screened I-UNCLEAR; the emphasized quantitative classical comparison is compliance against the voxel-based density method, Sec. 5.4 and Fig. 6; the iteration counts are disclosed as a cost limitation)

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: On three 2D benchmarks (MBB 300×100, roof 180×180, bridge 250×125), ENDR designs have lower compliance than the voxel-based density method (285.7 vs 316.7; 2.731 vs 2.905; 9.732 vs 9.785), using 5000 iterations against about 300.
claim.key_phrase: quantitatively match or exceed the results of two state-of-the-art methods
claim.location: Sec. 5.4 (p. 6) and Fig. 6 (p. 7). The abstract (p. 1) and conclusion (Sec. 7, p. 7) compare with standard methods only qualitatively ('state-of-the-art performance'; 'outperform or be on par with standard FEM-based solutions in terms of stiffness'); chosen under §5.1 rules 2 and 4 as the comparison the article emphasizes, over the iteration counts of the same paragraph, which the article presents as a cost limitation (alternative 1)
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: Not applicable: the primary outcome compares design quality only. No wall-clock time of the voxel-based or CNN baselines is reported anywhere (Sec. 5.4, 5.6). The only cost comparison is an iteration count, about 300 for the baselines against the 5000 iterations ENDR is restricted to (Sec. 5.4, p. 6), a ratio of 0.06 [derived], i.e. ENDR needs about 16.7 times more iterations; recorded as alternative 1.
claim.alternatives: (1) Sec. 5.4 (p. 6): ENDR is restricted to 5000 iterations, while the voxel-based and CNN methods 'fully converge in around 300 iterations'; iteration ratio 300/5000 = 0.06 [derived], a slowdown the article calls the cost of the method (Sec. 5.4) and its primary limitation (Sec. 6). If a verifier takes this as primary, the record moves to the speed stratum with direction underperform and R3 = na (per-problem learning). (2) Sec. 5.3 and Fig. 5 (pp. 5-6): an ENDR design computed at 300×100 is upsampled and used to initialize the voxel-based method; the compliance reduction J_diff of that refinement (plotted, about 0-40) measures how near-optimal the upsampled design is. (3) Fig. 6 against the CNN parameterization of Hoyer et al. 2019 (ML, not classical): 285.7 vs 293.6, 2.731 vs 2.716, 9.732 vs 9.567, mixed. (4) Sec. 6 (p. 6): 5000 iterations against fewer than 200 for NTopo (Zehnder et al. 2021), an ML-vs-ML comparison. (5) Sec. 5.6 (p. 6): ENDR per-iteration solve times (2D 0.161 s and 0.164 s; 3D 5.74 s and 2.84 s) without a paired classical time.

baseline.classical_method: Traditional voxel-based density TO (element-center densities, SIMP p = 3, smoothing filter of radius 1 voxel) following Andreassen et al. 2011 (Sec. 3.2 and 5.4); the update rule is not stated for the Fig. 6 runs [inferred OC, as in the 88-line code]. A second, non-classical comparator (Hoyer et al. 2019's CNN reparameterization, filter radius 2) is benchmarked alongside it in Sec. 5.4
baseline.implementation: Voxel-based baseline follows Andreassen et al. 2011, run with a filter radius of 1 voxel (Sec. 5.4); whether the 88-line MATLAB code itself or the authors' own FEM pipeline was used is not stated. The CNN baseline follows Hoyer et al. 2019 with filter radius 2, 'the default value in the original paper' (Sec. 5.4)
baseline.solver: Sparse Cholesky factorization for 2D problems; multigrid-preconditioned conjugate-gradient solver (3 coarsening levels, 2 Gauss-Seidel smoothing iterations per level, based on Wu et al. 2016) for 3D problems (Sec. 5.6) - both are efficient solver classes per the protocol's definition. Whether the voxel-based/CNN baselines in Sec. 5.4 use the identical solver is not stated explicitly [inferred: likely, given the shared FEM pipeline]
baseline.hardware_classical: Not stated separately from the ML hardware; one hardware description covers 'all benchmarks': Nvidia Quadro RTX 8000 GPU and AMD Ryzen 5950X CPU (Sec. 5.6)
baseline.hardware_ml: Same machine: Nvidia Quadro RTX 8000 GPU (network evaluation, when GPU memory allows) and AMD Ryzen 5950X CPU (Sec. 5.6); for higher-resolution designs, network operations can fall back to CPU due to GPU memory limits, becoming a timing bottleneck
baseline.problem_size: 2D comparison (Fig. 6): MBB beam 300×100 (V0 = 0.3), roof 180×180 (V0 = 0.4), bridge 250×125 (V0 = 0.4). 3D: cantilever 256×128×128 and bridge 320×160×80 (Sec. 5.5-5.6, Figs. 7-9), ENDR only. Network: 4 layers, 256 (2D) or 512 (3D) neurons/layer, 1024 Fourier features (Sec. 5.1)
baseline.classical_iterations: Voxel-based and CNN baselines 'fully converge in around 300 iterations' (Sec. 5.4); their stopping rule for Fig. 6 is not stated (Eq. 5, tol = 1e-7, is given only for the voxel-based refinement in the upsampling study, Sec. 5.3). ENDR is run for 5,000 iterations by default (Sec. 5.1, 5.4), except the specific 3D examples in Figs. 7-9, which used 2,700-3,500 iterations (figure captions)
baseline.classical_time: Not stated as a standalone wall-clock number for the voxel-based/CNN baselines
baseline.ml_time: Average per-iteration FEM-solve time: 2D, 0.161 s (300x100 MBB beam) and 0.164 s (250x125 bridge) via sparse Cholesky (Sec. 5.6); 3D, 5.74 s (320x160x80 bridge) and 2.84 s (256x128x128 cantilever) via multigrid-CG (Sec. 5.6). Network evaluation/backpropagation adds further time per iteration, approaching but not exceeding the elasticity-solve time; total run length is 5,000 iterations by default (2,700-3,500 for the specific 3D examples shown)
baseline.training_time: Not applicable in the offline sense: ENDR is optimized from scratch for each new problem ('self-supervised pipeline does not depend on labeled data', Sec. 4.2); its optimization cost is the per-run, per-iteration cost above, run for 5,000 iterations by default
baseline.data_generation_cost: Not applicable: no labeled dataset is used; network weights are optimized directly against analytical compliance/volume gradients for each new problem (Sec. 4.2, Eq. 2)
baseline.quality_metric: Compliance J of the returned design, computed with the same FEM model used during optimization (Sec. 3.1, 4.2; values printed in Fig. 6); volume enforced as a soft one-sided penalty that 'generally' keeps the violation below 1e-4 (Sec. 4.3)
baseline.quality_gap: Fig. 6 (p. 7), ENDR vs voxel-based: MBB 285.7 vs 316.7 (9.8% lower [derived]); roof 2.731 vs 2.905 (6.0% lower [derived]); bridge 9.732 vs 9.785 (0.5% lower [derived]). Against the CNN (ML): 293.6, 2.716 and 9.567, so ENDR is lower in one case of three. Achieved volumes are not reported per case

R1.evidence: Sec. 5.4 (p. 6) and Fig. 6 (p. 7): R1 applies as written in stratum Q (PROTOCOL §11). Both methods solve the same three problems at the same volume budgets, and compliances are printed; no fail marker applies, because no time is compared. Matching is loose: ENDR gets 5000 iterations against the voxel method's ~300; ENDR's volume is a soft penalty 'generally' within 1e-4 (Sec. 4.3, p. 4), with no per-case volume reported; and the voxel method's stopping rule for Fig. 6 is not stated (Eq. 5 covers only the upsampling runs of Sec. 5.3). This is the §5.3 R1 partial case.

R2.evidence: Stratum Q (PROTOCOL §11, 2026-09-24): R2 applies only through criterion (b). The abstract (p. 1) names no baseline and gives no numbers ('state-of-the-art performance'), so it cannot report a weaker baseline than Sec. 5.4 and Fig. 6; (b) does not apply. For reference: the voxel-based baseline follows Andreassen et al. 2011 with filter radius 1 and converges in about 300 iterations (Sec. 5.4); the authors' own solves use sparse Cholesky (2D) and multigrid-preconditioned CG (3D) (Sec. 5.6).

R3.evidence: Stratum Q (PROTOCOL §11): R3 concerns speed claims and is na. It would be na in any case: ENDR is a per-instance, self-supervised optimization with no dataset and no offline training (Sec. 4.2), the §5.3 per-problem case.

R4.evidence: The compliance of each returned ENDR design is computed with the same FEM model used during optimization (Sec. 3.1, 4.2, pp. 2-3; J values printed in Fig. 6, p. 7), not with an image metric or a surrogate. Volume satisfaction is stated only as a general bound (violation 'generally' below 1e-4, Sec. 4.3, p. 4), not per case, and no failure, disconnection or infeasibility count is reported for the comparison or upsampling results.

reporting.n_test_cases: Classical comparison: 3 2D problems (MBB 300×100, roof 180×180, bridge 250×125; Fig. 6), one run each [inferred]. Other studies: a frequency-sweep study (Fig. 2, 6 σ values), a filter-radius comparison (Fig. 3), a mesh-independence study across 3 resolutions (Fig. 4), an upsampling study (Fig. 5, one source resolution upsampled to several targets), 3D examples (Figs. 7-9), density-space OC experiments (Fig. 10)

notes: No author named Jun Wang. The reference list cites 'Jun Wu, Christian Dick, and Rudiger Westermann. 2016. A System for High-Resolution Topology Optimization' (the source of the 3D multigrid-CG solver used here) - this is Jun Wu, a different surname from Jun Wang, and in any case a cited reference rather than an author of this article, so it does not trigger the Jun Wang flag. Duplicate check via audit/pool/pool.csv title search: only one matching row (P00842 itself); no duplicate found. Access notes: the ACM Digital Library page (dl.acm.org) returned HTTP 403 to automated access, so it was not used (no bot check was bypassed); the PDF was instead obtained from a co-author's institutional page (Max Planck Institute for Informatics), a legal author-hosted copy explicitly marked on its cover page as 'the author's version of the work ... posted here for your personal use'. Code/data check: no code- or data-availability statement appears in the article, and the corresponding author's own publication page (julianpanetta.com/publication/topoptndr) lists only a PDF link, no code link specific to this paper, so code_available and retest_candidate are set to no/false. Screening code was I-UNCLEAR. Adjudication (2026-09-24): the first coder met the ACM Cloudflare check and coded abstract-only; the adjudicator read the author's version in full and based the record on the second coding, but changed the primary outcome. The second coder took the iteration contrast (300 vs 5000) as primary, describing the Fig. 6 compliance comparison as qualitative only; Fig. 6 in fact prints the compliance of every design, the abstract, Sec. 5.4 and the conclusion emphasize stiffness, and the iteration count is presented as a limitation. The record therefore moves to stratum Q, with claimed_speedup null, R2 and R3 na under the §11 stratum-Q reading, and the baseline quality_gap filled from Fig. 6.

access.reason: The author's version on co-author Babaei's MPI Informatics group page (aidam.mpi-inf.mpg.de/data/pdfs/toftndr.pdf) is a legal author copy; it returned HTTP 200 with no challenge and was read in full (9 pp.). The first coder tried only the ACM PDF, which serves a Cloudflare check.

stratum.reason: The abstract (p. 1) and conclusion (Sec. 7, p. 7) compare with standard methods only qualitatively, and on stiffness. In the main text, Sec. 5.4 (p. 6) opens with ENDR matching or exceeding the voxel-based method, quantified in Fig. 6 (p. 7: 285.7 vs 316.7, 2.731 vs 2.905, 9.732 vs 9.785); the 300 vs 5000 iteration counts follow as the cost of that performance. Under §5.1 rules 2 and 4 the emphasized outcome compares design quality only, so the stratum is quality.

claimed_speedup.reason: The primary outcome is a compliance comparison, and no wall-clock time of the voxel-based baseline is reported (Sec. 5.4, 5.6, p. 6). The iteration ratio 300/5000 = 0.06 [derived] is kept as alternative 1, not as a speed-up.

R1.reason: R1 applies as written in stratum Q (§11), and no time is compared, so no fail marker holds. Matching is loose: ENDR gets 5000 iterations against the baseline's ~300 (Sec. 5.4, p. 6), its volume is only a soft penalty 'generally' within 1e-4 (Sec. 4.3, p. 4) with no per-case report, and the baseline's stopping rule for Fig. 6 is not stated. The second coder reached partial on a wrong premise (that no compliance numbers are printed); Fig. 6 prints them.

R2.reason: In stratum Q, R2 is na unless criterion (b) applies (PROTOCOL §11). The abstract (p. 1) names no baseline and gives no numbers, so it cannot report a weaker baseline than Sec. 5.4 and Fig. 6.

R3.reason: R3 is na in stratum Q (§11), and ENDR is in any case optimized per problem with no dataset or offline training (Sec. 4.2, p. 3).

R4.reason: Each returned design's compliance comes from the same FEM model (Sec. 3.1, 4.2; Fig. 6, p. 7), but volume satisfaction is only a general bound ('generally' below 1e-4, Sec. 4.3, p. 4) and no failure or disconnection count is reported: the §5.3 R4 partial case.
